Right now, November 2025, the International Court of Justice is hearing oral arguments. The ruling comes in 2027. I analyzed three past ICJ border rulings to see what the court actually does when countries claim colonial treaties should be void.

The precedent points toward one likely outcome: The ICJ will probably confirm Belize's boundary. But the legal reasoning matters, and neither Guatemala nor Belize is seeing this clearly.

The 1859 Wyke-Aycinena Treaty established the boundary in Article 1 with specific coordinates. Article 7 said Britain would use "best efforts" to build a road from Guatemala City to the Atlantic coast. Britain never built it.

The legal test comes from the Vienna Convention on the Law of Treaties, Article 60: Was the broken promise "essential to the accomplishment of the object or purpose of the treaty"?

The ruling will set precedent for how the ICJ interprets colonial treaties where one party claims the agreement was conditional and unfulfilled.

GuL9PtXEjN0.title: Somaliland's Legal Independence Problem
GuL9PtXEjN0.description:
In 1960, 35 countries recognized Somaliland as an independent state. Then they all forgot. This is the legal case the world pretends doesn't exist.

On June 26, 1960, the Somaliland Order in Council granted independence to British Somaliland—making it a recognized state for five days before a planned merger with Italian Somalia. But the merger treaty was never properly signed. In 1963, a British judge ruled the union had no legal basis. In 2005, the African Union's own fact-finding mission called Somaliland's case "historically unique and self-justified in African political history."

  So why does the international community still refuse recognition?

  The Documents

1960 Independence (June 26): British Somaliland Order in Council 1960 granted full independence. 35+ states extended formal recognition through bilateral agreements, including the US, USSR, China, UK, France, Egypt, Ethiopia, Ghana, and Israel.

The Failed Union (July 1): Two separate parliaments passed two different union laws—neither signed by both parties. Somalia's Act of Union was approved "in principle" but never enacted into law. Legal scholar Eugene Cotran documented this defect in his 1961 analysis.

1963 Court Ruling: British Judge Hazelwood ruled that "in the absence of an Act of Union, the court had no jurisdiction over Somaliland." Somalia attempted retroactive validation through Law No. 5 (1961), but scholars debate whether you can retroactively cure a void agreement.

2005 AU Investigation: African Union fact-finding mission concluded: "The fact that the union between Somaliland and Somalia was never ratified makes Somaliland's search for recognition historically unique and self-justified in African political history." The AU recommended finding a "special method" to deal with this case. No action was taken.

2024-2025 Developments: Ethiopia signed a port access deal (January 2024) with language about "in-depth assessment towards recognition." Israel became the first UN member to formally recognize Somaliland (December 2025), triggering immediate AU rejection.

  Why This Matters

  Somaliland isn't arguing it should become independent—it's arguing it already was. The documentary evidence supports this: the 1960 independence order, 35+ recognitions, the never-ratified treaty, the 1963 court ruling, and the AU's own 2005 investigation.

  The question isn't whether the legal case exists. It's whether the international community will read the documents they already have.

LuLZYZWMiU4.title: The Flat Earth Myth Was Invented in 1828. Here's Who Did It.
LuLZYZWMiU4.description:
The flat earth myth was invented in 1828. Here's who did it—and why schools still teach it.

You probably learned that medieval people thought the earth was flat until Columbus proved them wrong. That story appears in textbooks, Hollywood movies, and modern conspiracy theories.

It's completely fabricated.

I went through the medieval manuscripts—Bede (725 AD), Sacrobosco (1230), the royal orb held by kings—and traced this lie to three specific men who invented it between 1828 and 1896.


THE MEDIEVAL EVIDENCE

Medieval scholars explicitly described a spherical earth:

• Bede (725 AD): "The earth resembles more a ball, being equally round in all directions"
• Isidore of Seville (630 AD): Defined night as "the sun under the earth"—impossible on a flat disc
• Johannes de Sacrobosco's Tractatus de Sphaera (c. 1230): Standard university astronomy textbook for 400 years, surviving in hundreds of manuscripts
• The globus cruciger—a royal orb showing a cross atop a sphere—appeared in European coronation ceremonies from the 11th century

This wasn't fringe. This was mainstream medieval knowledge.


THE FABRICATION TIMELINE (1828-1896)

Three men turned fiction into textbook fact:

1. Washington Irving (1828): A novelist—not a historian—invented the Salamanca scene in his Columbus biography. He fabricated "ignorant monks" citing the Bible to prove the earth was flat. That scene never happened.

2. John William Draper (1874): Published "History of the Conflict Between Religion and Science" during the culture wars after Darwin. Turned Irving's fiction into anti-Catholic propaganda. 50+ printings.

3. Andrew Dickson White (1896): Cornell's co-founder buried the lie under a mountain of footnotes, giving it academic respectability.

Between 1870 and 1920, this fabrication entered every textbook.

---

WHY IT PERSISTS

Historian Jeffrey Burton Russell debunked this in 1991. It didn't matter.

The lie persists because:
• It's simple, dramatic, emotionally satisfying
• It serves the "Dark Ages vs Enlightenment" narrative
• Modern flat earthers now use it as evidence that "experts always lie"

The supreme irony: 19th-century anticlerical academics invented this myth to build up science's authority. Today, populist movements use it to tear science down.

TYNaIu28LeU.title: The 1922 Treaty Loophole That Ended the USSR
TYNaIu28LeU.description:
In December 1991, three leaders met in a Viskuli hunting lodge to sign the ending of a superpower. But one fact is often ignored: just months earlier, 78% of voters in the March Referendum had voted to preserve the USSR.
This video analyzes the legal text of the Belavezha Accords against Article 72 of the Soviet Constitution and the 1922 Treaty of Creation to determine if the dissolution was a legal act of secession or an unconstitutional coup.

Was that legal?

This video examines the actual Belavezha Accords—the 1991 document Russia now uses to argue Ukraine's borders were never legitimate—and asks whether the dissolution of the Soviet Union followed its own laws.

THE EVIDENCE EXAMINED:
• The Belavezha Preamble: "as Founder States... we hereby declare..."
• Article 5: The territorial integrity clause Russia later violated
• Article 14: The provision that terminated all Soviet institutions
• The 1990 Secession Law the signers bypassed
• The March 1991 referendum they overruled
• The 1922 Treaty of Creation—and the "founder states" loophole

THE VERDICT:
Under Soviet law, almost certainly unconstitutional. But historically? The Accords formalized the end of a state that was already collapsing.

WHY THIS MATTERS NOW:
In August 1991—four months before Belavezha—Yeltsin's press secretary named two regions Russia would claim if republics left: Crimea and the Donbas.

In 2022, Russia invaded Ukraine.
In 2025, a Putin adviser declared the USSR "still legally exists."

The Belavezha question isn't academic. It's the legal argument behind a war.

P6yalauLDic.description:
Bermeja is a phantom island off Mexico's Yucatan coast that appeared on maps for 382 years — from the 1539 Santa Cruz atlas to Mexico's official charts in 2009. It was never there.

When Mexico needed Bermeja to anchor its maritime boundary and claim oil fields in the Gulf's "donut hole," the Navy sailed to its coordinates and found nothing but deep ocean. The US-Mexico treaty was signed without it. Mexican senators accused the CIA of destroying the island. UNAM's 2009 expedition proved no island had existed at those coordinates for over 5,300 years.

This is the story of the most expensive cartographic error in history.

What you'll see in this video:
- The 1539 atlas that created the phantom island
- How 16th-century navigation errors became permanent map features
- The 2000 US-Mexico treaty that divided the Gulf oil
- The CIA conspiracy theory — and the geology that kills it
